case_study_insert.main_stem: Saffron Spice Grill (SSG) is a partnership in the hospitality sector, running a chain of four casual-dining restaurants and employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Nadia Rahman, the business has a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. SSG plans to invest $380,000 in two new city-centre branches, financed by a $150,000 bank loan and $230,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $182,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $38, and produces 22,000 units a year, where each unit is one meal served. SSG faces rising food-waste levels and 10% absenteeism among its kitchen staff, with repeat bookings falling in its four branches.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Kitchen Quality Report — Q4 2025: SSG served 18,000 meals across its four branches. Food waste was 8% of ingredients purchased, down from 11% a year earlier, and customer complaints fell to 44 from 61 per month. Average table turnaround was 52 minutes, with 95% of orders delivered within 15 minutes of ordering. A survey of 800 diners gave SSG a 4.3/5 rating, and 56% said value for money was good. A skills check found 7 of 35 staff had not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the local college costs $650 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Saffron Spice Grill as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Dining Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of business borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.02 to $13.95 an hour, pushing up kitchen payroll costs. (3) Food input inflation reached 11.2% year-on-year, while consumer spending on eating out grew 2.8%.

questions.question_text: SSG is funding its $380,000 expansion with a $150,000 bank loan and $230,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for SSG of taking the bank loan instead of relying solely on retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Taking a $150,000 bank loan preserves SSG's cash reserve instead of spending all $230,000 of retained profit at once. That matters for a partnership with fixed costs of $182,000 a year and food waste of 8% of ingredients: cash kept back can absorb the 11.2% rise in food input costs and pay the 7.2% higher wages without delaying the two new city-centre branches.

Point 2: The loan lets both branches open together rather than forcing Nadia Rahman to sequence the $380,000 project around whatever retained profit accumulates. Opening together captures the 2.8% growth in eating-out spending sooner and spreads the $12 variable cost across 22,000 meals, so the $38 selling price and $26 contribution start covering the added fixed costs earlier. Borrowing also leaves the partners' own capital untouched, and the 4.3/5 rating from 800 diners and 56% who say value for money is good support the extra demand needed to service the loan. Retaining the $230,000 instead would leave less room to absorb the 7.2% wage rise during the launch of both branches.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SSG's expansion financing.

questions.question_text: SSG wants to attract diners to its two new city-centre branches. Consider a local radio campaign, leaflet drops, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SSG choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio: Radio reaches commuters and nearby office workers during the day, which could fill the 52-minute table turnaround at lunch, and it is cheaper than television. However, audio cannot show SSG's food, and a 5.0% base rate makes borrowing for promotion less attractive; the 800-diner survey shows 56% already judge value for money good, so the message must be visual and specific.

Leaflet drops: Doorstep leaflets with vouchers are cheap and can be targeted at neighbourhoods around the new branches, encouraging first visits and helping lift repeat bookings. Their weaknesses are low response rates and environmental waste that sits awkwardly with a business already trying to cut its 8% food waste; leaflets also do nothing to communicate the 4.3/5 rating to diners beyond the immediate delivery area.

Social media influencer marketing: Food influencers can photograph dishes and show the 4.3/5 rating and 56% value-for-money verdict to a large, relevant local audience, with engagement that can be tracked against the 18,000 meals baseline. Results build over time and depend on choosing credible reviewers, but cost per diner is low and the content can highlight improvements that cut the 44 monthly complaints.

Recommendation: SSG should choose social media influencer marketing, with small leaflet vouchers for launch week only. It shows the food, leverages the strong diner survey and reaches beyond a single radio catchment at a cost that fits a $150,000 loan-funded expansion. Radio is rejected because it cannot display the product, and leaflets are rejected as a main channel because of low response and waste concerns.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SSG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SSG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and leaflets are rejected.

questions.question_text: SSG's absenteeism has reached 10% and food-waste levels are rising. Explain two benefits for SSG of introducing job rotation in its kitchens.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves the workforce of 35 between preparation, cooking and service, reducing repetition and boredom in a laissez-faire setting where staff otherwise get little variety. Higher job satisfaction should cut the 10% absenteeism, so kitchens stay fully staffed and the 95% of orders delivered within 15 minutes can be maintained, protecting the 4.3/5 rating from 800 diners.

Point 2: Rotation gives Nadia Rahman's staff a wider range of skills, so cover is available when a chef is absent and the 52-minute table turnaround does not lengthen. Staff who work across stations can spot food-waste at each stage, helping cut the current 8% waste and the 44 monthly complaints; this supports the $38 selling price and $26 contribution needed to service the $150,000 bank loan as two new branches open. Nadia Rahman can check absence and the 44 monthly complaints after a trial before extending rotation to all four branches, keeping the flat structure intact.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SSG's absenteeism, waste, service times and expansion.

questions.question_text: SSG must train 7 of 35 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should SSG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Kitchen coaching is tailored to SSG's own recipes, portion standards and the 52-minute turnaround, costs no fees, and keeps the 7 trainees productive. It can directly reduce the 8% food waste and the 44 monthly complaints because supervisors correct practice immediately. Drawbacks are that busy chefs have little time to teach, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate, which may matter as the partnership opens two new branches with consistent standards.

Off-the-job training: The local college course costs $650 per employee, so 7 × $650 = $4,550, small beside the $380,000 investment. It provides structured hygiene and supervisory skills and a recognised certificate, useful for a growing four-branch chain. However, it pulls 7 of 35 staff out of kitchens during service, risking the 95% on-time order record and longer than 52 minutes at tables, and generic content will still need on-site adaptation to SSG's menu.

Decision: SSG should choose on-the-job training first, followed by short college hygiene modules. It is cheaper, specific to SSG's kitchens and avoids disrupting service while 10% absenteeism is already stretching a workforce of 35. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the lost kitchen shifts and the $4,550 fee would hit the 18,000-meal operation, and the new branches need consistent on-site standards immediately. A short trial in one branch would show whether the 52-minute turnaround, the 44 monthly complaints and the 8% food waste improve before SSG spends $4,550 on all 7 trainees, with Nadia Rahman reviewing the results across the four branches.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SSG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of SSG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, service disruption and kitchen relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SSG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate SSG's average total cost per meal.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = Fixed cost per unit + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $182,000 ÷ 22,000 = $8.27, plus $12 = $20.27. Answer: average total cost is $20.27 a meal.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38 − $12 = $26. Answer: contribution per unit is $26.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SSG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Average total cost of $20.27 against a $38 selling price shows a $17.73 margin a meal, giving partners a clear benchmark for the two new branches and for the 8% food-waste reduction target.
2. Contribution of $26 lets managers test pricing: a $2 discount to $36 leaves $24 contribution, so they can judge whether extra diners compensate before using vouchers to lift the 56% value-for-money rating.
3. With fixed costs of $182,000 and $26 contribution, break-even is $182,000 ÷ $26 = 7,000 meals, a target for each new branch against the 18,000 meals already served across four sites.
4. Managers can compare unit cost with the $650 per employee training fee and 10% absenteeism to see whether cutting 7 untrained staff's errors on the 44 monthly complaints is worth the spend, and renegotiate the $12 variable cost given 11.2% food inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Average total cost = $20.27 | (ii) Contribution per unit = $26 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: $20.27 cost versus $38 price; $26 contribution for discount and voucher decisions; break-even of 7,000 meals for new branches; and unit-cost benchmarking against $650 training and 11.2% food inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SSG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SSG's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.13 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.26 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.67 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.89 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $28,000 inventories + $18,000 trade receivables + $22,000 cash = $68,000; 2025 current assets = $24,000 + $30,000 + $28,000 = $82,000. For 2024, $68,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.13 and ($68,000 − $28,000) ÷ $60,000 = $40,000 ÷ $60,000 = 0.67. For 2025, $82,000 ÷ $65,000 = 1.26 and ($82,000 − $24,000) ÷ $65,000 = $58,000 ÷ $65,000 = 0.89.

Evaluation: Both measures improved, so short-term solvency is stronger. The first ratio rose from 1.13 to 1.26 despite current liabilities increasing from $60,000 to $65,000, because cash grew from $22,000 to $28,000 and inventories fell. The second measure climbed from 0.67 to 0.89, showing less dependence on selling the $24,000 of stock to meet bills, which is valuable while the partnership repays a $150,000 loan and spends $380,000 on two branches. Caution is still warranted: the 2025 second figure remains below 1, so liquid assets alone do not cover current liabilities, and trade receivables have risen from $18,000 to $30,000, tying up cash that could fund the 11.2% food-cost rise.

Conclusion: SSG's liquidity has improved, but only moderately. Both ratios rose and the improvement does not depend on inventory, yet the 0.89 figure leaves limited headroom, so the partners should tighten credit control on the higher receivables before committing further cash. Reviewing those balances monthly would protect the improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: SSG wants to reverse falling repeat bookings with a loyalty card scheme. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SSG of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A loyalty card rewards the 56% of 800 surveyed diners who already say value for money is good, encouraging repeat visits that lift the 18,000 meals baseline without heavy advertising. More meals spread the $182,000 fixed costs and protect the $26 contribution against 11.2% food input inflation, helping the two new branches reach break-even sooner.

Disadvantage: Discounts or free meals reduce the $38 average selling price and therefore the $26 contribution on rewarded visits, and the scheme needs tracking software and staff time that add to fixed costs while a $150,000 loan is outstanding. If rewards are too small they will not change behaviour; the insert gives no figure for redemption or setup cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified and the decision must be judged qualitatively. SSG should trial the card in one branch and compare repeat visits with the 800-diner survey before extending it to both new sites.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SSG's survey, meals, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% food input inflation will affect SSG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If SSG's $150,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $150,000 = $1,125 a year (0.0075 × $150,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $182,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. The higher rate could make future borrowing dearer and might slightly dampen the 2.8% growth in eating-out spending.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.95 an hour): SSG's workforce of 35 includes many hourly-paid kitchen and service staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or individual pay, so any annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 22,000 units ÷ 35 staff = about 628.6 meals per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; job rotation and training the 7 untrained staff can help maintain it.

Food input inflation (11.2%): This bears on the $12 variable cost of every meal. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $12 were exposed, 11.2% × $12 = $1.344, about $1.34 a meal, and at 22,000 units that is roughly $29,568 a year (22,000 × $1.344). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $26 contribution on each meal, and it recurs on every one of the 22,000 meals, unlike the one-off loan-interest figure.

Conclusion: Food input inflation will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 22,000 meals and directly erodes the $26 contribution that services the $150,000 loan and funds the $380,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,125 a year and the wage increase can be offset by sustaining 628.6 meals per worker. SSG should cut the 8% food waste and review the $38 price rather than absorb the whole rise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SSG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SSG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that food input inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
